title: People Who Changed the World: Relative Clauses in Biographical Writing
paragraphs: Biographical writing relies more heavily on relative clauses than almost any other genre. The reason is structural: when you write about a person, you constantly need to add information about them — who they were, what they did, when they did it, where they lived, whose ideas they built on. Relative clauses are the grammatical tool that allows you to incorporate this information within a sentence rather than breaking it into fragments.

Consider the difference between these two versions of the same information: Version A: "Marie Curie was a physicist. She discovered radium. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize." Version B: "Marie Curie, who discovered radium and who was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, was a physicist whose work transformed our understanding of radioactivity." Version B uses three relative clauses to create a single, coherent sentence. The information is the same; the effect is dramatically different.

The defining relative clause is used to identify which person or thing we mean. Without it, the sentence loses its meaning or becomes ambiguous. "The scientist who discovered penicillin changed medicine forever" — without "who discovered penicillin," we would not know which scientist is being referred to. The relative clause here is not extra information: it is essential information that defines the subject.

The non-defining relative clause, by contrast, adds information about a person or thing that has already been identified. "Alexander Fleming, who was working at St Mary's Hospital in 1928, noticed that bacteria near a mould had been killed." Fleming has already been identified by name, so the relative clause that follows is additional context — interesting, but not necessary to identify the subject. We signal this by surrounding the clause with commas.

The distinction between the two types has consequences that go beyond punctuation. In a defining relative clause, "that" can replace "who" or "which" in informal English: "The scientist that discovered penicillin" is acceptable in speech. But in a non-defining clause, "that" cannot be used: "Alexander Fleming, that worked at St Mary's Hospital" is wrong. The non-defining clause requires "who" for people and "which" for things.

Biographical writing at B1 and above uses both types fluidly. A biographer might write: "The discovery, which was made almost by accident, changed the course of modern medicine. Fleming, whose earlier work had focused on antiseptics, had been investigating ways to fight bacterial infections. It was a mould, specifically Penicillium notatum, which contaminated one of his petri dishes, that produced the antibacterial effect that he went on to study." This passage contains five relative clauses — each doing a different piece of structural work.

Reading these constructions with full comprehension requires not just knowing the grammar, but understanding why each clause was placed where it was — what question it answers, what additional meaning it creates, and whether its presence is essential or supplementary to the sentence's core meaning. That capacity — to read structure analytically — is one of the markers of B1+ reading comprehension.

dialogue.speaker: Daniyar
dialogue.text: I'm trying to write a biography of Abai for my literature essay. I keep producing lists of facts.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: That's the defining vs non-defining relative clause problem. You're writing "He was born in 1845. He studied in Semipalatinsk. He wrote the Book of Words." Each sentence is fine but they don't connect.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: "Abai, who was born in 1845 and who spent his formative years in Semipalatinsk, produced the Book of Words, which remains one of the foundational texts of Kazakh literature."

dialogue.speaker: Daniyar
dialogue.text: That's much better. The commas make the difference — the clauses feel like they belong.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Exactly. The commas say: "This is extra information. I've already told you who I'm talking about."

dialogue.speaker: Daniyar
dialogue.text: And without commas, the clause defines which one.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: "The poem that made him famous" — defines which poem. "The poem, which made him famous" — adds that extra information about an already-identified poem.

keyPhrases.context: "Essential information that defines the subject." = needed to identify which one.
"Adds information about an already-identified person." = extra, surrounded by commas.
"The noun that a relative pronoun refers back to."
"The sentence becomes ambiguous." = unclear, can be interpreted in more than one way.
"Incorporate information within a sentence." = include it as part of the structure.
"Rather than breaking into fragments." = short disconnected pieces.
"Essential or supplementary." = extra/extra detail, not the core meaning.
"Read structure analytically." = examine it carefully and think critically.
